claim: Multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is an increasing cause of infant mortality in developing countries.
source: Multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is an increasing cause of infant mortality in developing countries.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background claim about the clinical importance of the pathogen.

claim: All widely-used antibiotics except imipenem were associated with an increased daily acquisition risk of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae.
source: All widely-used antibiotics except imipenem were associated with an increased daily acquisition risk, with an odds ratio for the most common combination (ampicillin + gentamicin) of 1.96 (95% CrI 1.18, 3.36).
evidence: The abstract reports statistical findings from the study with specific odds ratios and credible intervals.

claim: The odds ratio for ampicillin + gentamicin on daily acquisition risk is 1.96 (95% CrI 1.18, 3.36).
source: All widely-used antibiotics except imipenem were associated with an increased daily acquisition risk, with an odds ratio for the most common combination (ampicillin + gentamicin) of 1.96 (95% CrI 1.18, 3.36).
evidence: Specific quantitative result from statistical modeling reported in the abstract.

claim: Colonisation pressure was associated with a higher transmission risk.
source: Models incorporating genomic data found that colonisation pressure was associated with a higher transmission risk, indicated sequence type heterogeneity in transmissibility, and showed that within-ward transmission was insufficient to maintain endemicity.
evidence: Finding from transmission models incorporating genomic data reported in the abstract.

claim: There is sequence type heterogeneity in transmissibility of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae.
source: Models incorporating genomic data found that colonisation pressure was associated with a higher transmission risk, indicated sequence type heterogeneity in transmissibility, and showed that within-ward transmission was insufficient to maintain endemicity.
evidence: Finding from genomic analysis and transmission modeling reported in the abstract.

claim: Within-ward transmission was insufficient to maintain endemicity of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae.
source: Models incorporating genomic data found that colonisation pressure was associated with a higher transmission risk, indicated sequence type heterogeneity in transmissibility, and showed that within-ward transmission was insufficient to maintain endemicity.
evidence: Finding from transmission modeling reported in the abstract.

claim: Increasing the nurse-patient ratio could be an effective intervention to reduce 3GC-R K. pneumoniae acquisition.
source: Simulations indicated that increasing the nurse-patient ratio could be an effective intervention.
evidence: Result from forward simulation modeling reported in the abstract.

claim: Extended spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) producing and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae have been prioritised by the World Health Organization as pathogenic bacteria in need of novel therapeutics.
source: Infections with multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae constitute a major threat to public health in all regions of the world (Schwaber and Carmeli, 2008; Theuretzbacher, 2017) and extended spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) producing and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae have been prioritised by the World Health Organization as pathogenic bacteria in need of novel therapeutics (World Health Organization, 2014; World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by WHO citations.

claim: Multidrug-resistant organisms pose the highest risk to subgroups of patients such as those undergoing surgery, requiring invasive devices, and neonates.
source: These organisms pose the highest risk to subgroups of patients such as those undergoing surgery, requiring invasive devices, and neonates (Peleg and Hooper, 2010; Goldmann, 1981).
evidence: Statement supported by literature citations.

claim: The estimated per capita mortality from drug-resistant bacteraemia is far greater in developing countries than in high-income countries.
source: Antimicrobial resistance is of particular concern in developing (lower and middle-income) countries where the estimated per capita mortality from drug-resistant bacteraemia is far greater than in high-income countries and where last-line antibiotics may be unavailable or unaffordable (Lim et al., 2016; Zaidi et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by literature citations.

claim: K. pneumoniae is amongst the most clinically important multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria in developing country settings.
source: In this paper, we focus on Klebsiella pneumoniae, which is amongst the most clinically important multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria in developing country settings (Fox-Lewis et al., 2018; Zellweger et al., 2017; Musicha et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Genomic studies have revealed that K. pneumoniae consists of three separate species (K. pneumoniae, K. quasipneumoniae, K. variicola) that are indistinguishable by culture or standard biochemical assays.
source: Genomic studies characterising the population structure of K. pneumoniae have revealed a complex consisting of three separate species (K. pneumoniae, K. quasipneumoniae, K. variicola) that are indistinguishable by culture or standard biochemical assays (Holt et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to genomic study.

claim: Research during the 1960s identified drivers of Klebsiella colonisation including invasive devices, environmental contamination, introduction from the community, person-to-person transmission, endogenous selection from antibiotic pressure, and transient carriage on the hands of health-care workers.
source: Research during the 1960s identified a number of drivers of Klebsiella colonisation and infection in hospital settings including invasive devices (Mertz et al., 1967), environmental contamination (Kresky, 1964), introduction from the community (Kessner and Lepper, 1967), person-to-person transmission (Weil et al., 1966), endogenous selection from antibiotic pressure (Selden et al., 1971) and transient carriage on the hands of health-care workers (Adler et al., 1970).
evidence: Historical research findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: The likely means of transmission of Klebsiella is via the hands of hospital staff members.
source: In a comprehensive review of this body of work, Montgomerie concluded that 'The likely means of transmission of Klebsiella is via the hands of hospital staff members' (Montgomerie, 1979).
evidence: Conclusion from a comprehensive review cited.

claim: Prospective carriage studies in hospitalised paediatric populations in developing countries have reported hyperendemic levels of ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae including K. pneumoniae.
source: In contrast to studies in high-income countries where multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae is typically rare, prospective carriage studies in hospitalised paediatric populations in developing countries in Africa and Asia have reported hyperendemic levels of ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae including K. pneumoniae (Andriatahina et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2019; Founou et al., 2019; Turner et al., 2016) consistent with the greater burden of disease due to these organisms in lower income settings (Lim et al., 2016; Musicha et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple study citations.

claim: Recent investigations of localised hospital outbreaks in high-income settings have provided evidence that long-term environmental contamination of sinks and other sites may play a role in K. pneumoniae transmission.
source: First, while a number of recent investigations of localised hospital outbreaks in high-income settings have provided evidence that long-term environmental contamination of sinks and other sites may play a role (Clarivet et al., 2016; Decraene et al., 2018; Mathers et al., 2018), the relative importance of persistently contaminated point sources versus patient-to-patient transmission in endemic settings remains unclear.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple outbreak investigation citations.

claim: Of 333 infants admitted to the neonatal unit, 121 of 289 (42%) were found to be colonised with 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. on the first swab taken within 48 hours of ward admission.
source: Of 333 infants admitted to the neonatal unit, 121 of 289 (42%) were found to be colonised on the first swab taken within 48 hours of ward admission.
evidence: Descriptive epidemiological data from the study.

claim: 109 out of 191 (57%) infants who initially screened negative for 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. became positive during their stay in the neonatal unit.
source: Overall, 109/191 (57%) infants who initially screened negative for 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. became positive during their stay in the neonatal unit.
evidence: Descriptive epidemiological data from the study.

claim: Almost all 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. isolates were ESBL producers (1412/1423; 99%).
source: Almost all 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. isolates were ESBL producers (1412/1423; 99%), and only 5/1423 (0.35%) were resistant to imipenem.
evidence: Microbiological characterization data from the study.

claim: Only 5/1423 (0.35%) of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. isolates were resistant to imipenem.
source: Almost all 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. isolates were ESBL producers (1412/1423; 99%), and only 5/1423 (0.35%) were resistant to imipenem.
evidence: Microbiological characterization data from the study.

claim: The median length of stay in the neonatal unit was 6 days (IQR 4, 11).
source: Length of Stay in Days Median, (IQR)*	**6 (4, 11)
evidence: Descriptive statistics from Table 1.

claim: The most frequently used antibiotic combination was ampicillin with gentamicin which was used on one fifth (19%) of patient days on the ward.
source: The most frequently used antibiotic combination was ampicillin with gentamicin which was used empirically to treat suspected sepsis in infants admitted from the community and was taken on one fifth (19%) of patient days on the ward.
evidence: Descriptive data on antibiotic usage from the study.

claim: Imipenem was taken on 12% of patient days.
source: This was followed by imipenem, which was taken on 12% of patient days.
evidence: Descriptive data on antibiotic usage from the study.

claim: Breast milk feeding was associated with reduced daily risk of acquisition (OR 0.69 [95% CrI 0.35, 1.41]).
source: The covariates associated with reduced daily risk of acquisition were breast milk feeding (odds ratio [OR] 0.69 [95% CrI 0.35, 1.41]) and increasing the number of nurses, for instance three nurses in the ward was associated with an OR of 0.55 (95% CrI 0.15, 1.77) relative to zero nurses (baseline).
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Increasing the number of nurses was associated with reduced daily risk of acquisition, with three nurses in the ward associated with an OR of 0.55 (95% CrI 0.15, 1.77) relative to zero nurses.
source: The covariates associated with reduced daily risk of acquisition were breast milk feeding (odds ratio [OR] 0.69 [95% CrI 0.35, 1.41]) and increasing the number of nurses, for instance three nurses in the ward was associated with an OR of 0.55 (95% CrI 0.15, 1.77) relative to zero nurses (baseline).
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Male sex was associated with a reduced risk of acquisition (OR 0.68 [95% CrI 0.43, 1.04]).
source: Male sex was also associated with a reduced risk of acquisition (OR 0.68 [95% CrI 0.43, 1.04]).
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Ampicillin was associated with an increased risk of colonisation (OR 1.77 [95% CrI 0.88, 3.26]).
source: Ampicillin (OR 1.77 [95% CrI 0.88, 3.26]), ampicillin with gentamicin (OR 1.96 [95% CrI 1.18, 3.36]), ceftriaxone (OR 1.85 [95% CrI 0.68, 4.54]), oral cloxacillin (OR 1.49 95% CrI 0.47, 4.02]), and cloxacillin with gentamicin (OR 1.94 [95% CrI 0.55, 5.66]) were all associated with an increased risk of acquisition.
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Ceftriaxone was associated with an increased risk of colonisation (OR 1.85 [95% CrI 0.68, 4.54]).
source: Ampicillin (OR 1.77 [95% CrI 0.88, 3.26]), ampicillin with gentamicin (OR 1.96 [95% CrI 1.18, 3.36]), ceftriaxone (OR 1.85 [95% CrI 0.68, 4.54]), oral cloxacillin (OR 1.49 95% CrI 0.47, 4.02]), and cloxacillin with gentamicin (OR 1.94 [95% CrI 0.55, 5.66]) were all associated with an increased risk of acquisition.
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Oral cloxacillin was associated with an increased risk of colonisation (OR 1.49 [95% CrI 0.47, 4.02]).
source: Ampicillin (OR 1.77 [95% CrI 0.88, 3.26]), ampicillin with gentamicin (OR 1.96 [95% CrI 1.18, 3.36]), ceftriaxone (OR 1.85 [95% CrI 0.68, 4.54]), oral cloxacillin (OR 1.49 95% CrI 0.47, 4.02]), and cloxacillin with gentamicin (OR 1.94 [95% CrI 0.55, 5.66]) were all associated with an increased risk of acquisition.
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Cloxacillin with gentamicin was associated with an increased risk of colonisation (OR 1.94 [95% CrI 0.55, 5.66]).
source: Ampicillin (OR 1.77 [95% CrI 0.88, 3.26]), ampicillin with gentamicin (OR 1.96 [95% CrI 1.18, 3.36]), ceftriaxone (OR 1.85 [95% CrI 0.68, 4.54]), oral cloxacillin (OR 1.49 95% CrI 0.47, 4.02]), and cloxacillin with gentamicin (OR 1.94 [95% CrI 0.55, 5.66]) were all associated with an increased risk of acquisition.
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: Intravenous imipenem had an odds ratio of 1.01 [0.40, 2.30] for acquisition risk, with a posterior distribution centred near unity.
source: Only intravenous imipenem (OR 1.01 [0.40, 2.30]) had a posterior distribution centred near unity, consistent with the carbapenem sensitivity of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae found in this setting.
evidence: Statistical modeling result from risk factor analysis.

claim: The median daily probability of first acquisition of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. for an infant was estimated as 0.15.
source: The median daily probability of first acquisition of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. for an infant was estimated from the best fitting model as 0.15.
evidence: Statistical modeling result.

claim: The medians of the posterior probability distribution for daily acquisition risk ranges nearly eight-fold from 0.047 to 0.35.
source: There is considerable variability in the risk of acquisition between patient days and the medians of the posterior probability distribution ranges nearly eight-fold from 0.047 to 0.35 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical modeling result with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The false negative rate posterior median for rectal swabs was 0.096 (95% CrI 0.078, 0.12) under the assumption that all negatives following a positive culture are false negatives.
source: Under the assumption that all negatives following a positive culture are false negatives, the false negative rate posterior median was 0.096 (95% CrI 0.078, 0.12) and the posterior median swab sensitivity was 0.90 (95% CrI 0.88, 0.92).
evidence: Statistical analysis of swab sensitivity.

claim: The posterior median swab sensitivity was 0.90 (95% CrI 0.88, 0.92) under the assumption that all negatives following a positive culture are false negatives.
source: Under the assumption that all negatives following a positive culture are false negatives, the false negative rate posterior median was 0.096 (95% CrI 0.078, 0.12) and the posterior median swab sensitivity was 0.90 (95% CrI 0.88, 0.92).
evidence: Statistical analysis of swab sensitivity.

claim: 62 distinct sequence types were identified in the collection of 317 isolates.
source: Overall 62 distinct sequence types were identified in our collection of isolates.
evidence: Genomic characterization data from the study.

claim: All three Klebsiella species (K. pneumoniae, K. quasipneumoniae subspecies similipneumoniae, K. variicola) were isolated from infants in the cohort.
source: We isolated all three species from infants in the cohort (K. pneumoniae n = 219, K. quasipneumoniae subspecies similipneumoniae n = 95, K. variicola n = 3), and found diversity similar to that observed in a global collection of K. pneumoniae isolates (Holt et al., 2015), suggesting that the diversity accumulated within a Cambodian neonatal unit over four months is comparable to the diversity of K. pneumoniae globally.
evidence: Genomic characterization data from the study.

claim: The diversity accumulated within a Cambodian neonatal unit over four months is comparable to the diversity of K. pneumoniae globally.
source: We isolated all three species from infants in the cohort (K. pneumoniae n = 219, K. quasipneumoniae subspecies similipneumoniae n = 95, K. variicola n = 3), and found diversity similar to that observed in a global collection of K. pneumoniae isolates (Holt et al., 2015), suggesting that the diversity accumulated within a Cambodian neonatal unit over four months is comparable to the diversity of K. pneumoniae globally.
evidence: Inference from comparison with global collection data.

claim: The STs with the largest number of carriage isolates were ST334 (n = 29), ST101 (n = 21), ST1074 (n = 21) and ST45 (n = 17).
source: The STs with the largest number of carriage isolates were ST334 (K. quasipneumoniae; n = 29), ST101 (K. pneumoniae; n = 21), ST1074 (K. pneumoniae; n = 21) and ST45 (K. pneumoniae; n = 17).
evidence: Genomic characterization data from the study.

claim: The most frequent blaESBL genes in the whole-genome assemblies were CTX-M-15 (201/317; 63%), followed by CTX-M-14 (43/317; 13%) and CTX-M-63 (38/317; 12%).
source: The most frequent blaESBL genes in the whole-genome assemblies were CTX-M-15 (201/317; 63%), followed by CTX-M-14 (43/317; 13%) and CTX-M-63 (38/317; 12%).
evidence: Genomic characterization data from the study.

claim: The model with the best fit to data by WAIC was transmission model 2, which has an intercept representing a constant risk of acquisition and a slope which scales the risk of acquisition for each infant colonised with a given ST in the ward.
source: Among transmission models 1–3 that were initially tested, the model with the best fit to data by WAIC was transmission model 2 (see Table 3 and Methods), which has an intercept (α), representing a constant risk of acquisition, and a slope (β) which scales the risk of acquisition for each infant colonised with a given ST in the ward (i.e. it accounts for colonisation pressure).
evidence: Model comparison result from transmission modeling.

claim: Transmission model 2 estimated α as 0.0019 (95% CrI 0.0015, 0.0023) and β as 0.0097 (95% CrI 0.0075, 0.012).
source: The model estimated the values for α as 0.0019 (95% CrI 0.0015, 0.0023) and β as 0.0097 (95% CrI 0.0075, 0.012).
evidence: Parameter estimates from transmission model 2.

claim: Transmission model 3 estimated λ as 4.7 (95% CrI [2.0, 7.0]), suggesting that contamination left by previously colonised infants decays rapidly to background levels.
source: Transmission model 3, which included terms for colonisation pressure and contamination in the hospital environment also failed to improve the model fit, and the high estimate for λ (4.7 95% CrI [2.0, 7.0]) suggests that contamination left by previously colonised infants decays rapidly to background levels, with an estimated environmental half life of 3.6 hours (95% CrI 2.4, 7.6 hours; Table 4).
evidence: Parameter estimate from transmission model 3 with interpretation.

claim: The estimated environmental half life of K. pneumoniae contamination is 3.6 hours (95% CrI 2.4, 7.6 hours).
source: Transmission model 3, which included terms for colonisation pressure and contamination in the hospital environment also failed to improve the model fit, and the high estimate for λ (4.7 95% CrI [2.0, 7.0]) suggests that contamination left by previously colonised infants decays rapidly to background levels, with an estimated environmental half life of 3.6 hours (95% CrI 2.4, 7.6 hours; Table 4).
evidence: Calculated from transmission model 3 parameter estimate.

claim: The pairwise number of variants in ST101 isolates between infants ranged from 15 to 68 SNPs (median 30).
source: The pairwise number of variants in ST101 isolates between infants ranged from 15 to 68 SNPs (median 30), which was comparable to the variation seen within infants in ST101 (from 18 to 38 SNPs; median 28).
evidence: Genomic analysis result from SNP diversity analysis.

claim: The within-host ST diversity in ST101 ranged from 18 to 38 SNPs (median 28).
source: The pairwise number of variants in ST101 isolates between infants ranged from 15 to 68 SNPs (median 30), which was comparable to the variation seen within infants in ST101 (from 18 to 38 SNPs; median 28).
evidence: Genomic analysis result from SNP diversity analysis.

claim: In ST45, the pairwise SNP differences between infants varied from 13 to 223 (median 125).
source: Similarly in ST45 the pairwise SNP differences between infants varied from 13 to 223 (median 125), which was comparable to the within-host ST diversity (from 55 to 212 SNPs; median 124).
evidence: Genomic analysis result from SNP diversity analysis.

claim: The within-host ST diversity in ST45 ranged from 55 to 212 SNPs (median 124).
source: Similarly in ST45 the pairwise SNP differences between infants varied from 13 to 223 (median 125), which was comparable to the within-host ST diversity (from 55 to 212 SNPs; median 124).
evidence: Genomic analysis result from SNP diversity analysis.

claim: The SNP diversity observed within and between-hosts was very similar for both ST45 and ST101.
source: Therefore the SNP diversity observed within and between-hosts was very similar for both ST45 and ST101.
evidence: Summary inference from SNP diversity analysis.

claim: The median of the ward-level reproduction number (RA) distribution was 0.65 and 95% of values fell between 0.36 and 1.09.
source: The median of the RA distribution was 0.65% and 95% of values fell between 0.36 and 1.09.
evidence: Result from agent-based simulation modeling.

claim: When the importation rate was high (40%), setting the proportion of infants taking the probiotic to 100% resulted in the median proportion remaining uncolonised as 0.59 (95% interval 0.39, 0.75).
source: When the importation rate was high (40% colonised on entry; similar to our study population, see Table 1), setting the proportion of infants taking the probiotic to be 0%, 50% or 100% resulted in the median proportion remaining uncolonised as 0.54 (95% interval 0.34, 0.72), 0.56 (95% interval 0.38, 0.72) and 0.59 (95% interval 0.39, 0.75) respectively.
evidence: Result from intervention simulation.

claim: Varying the number of nurses in the ward between three, four and eight in the high importation setting resulted in median proportions of initially uncolonised infants who remained uncolonised of 0.54, 0.61, and 0.81 respectively.
source: Varying the number of nurses in the ward between three, four and eight in the high importation setting resulted in median proportions of initially uncolonised infants who remained uncolonised throughout their neonatal unit stay of 0.54 (95% interval 0.36, 0.71), 0.61 (95% interval 0.39, 0.78) and 0.81 (95% interval 0.21, 0.97) respectively.
evidence: Result from intervention simulation.

claim: Of all the simulated interventions, increasing the number of nurses on the ward had the largest impact on reducing colonisation rates.
source: Of all the simulated interventions therefore, increasing the number of nurses on the ward had the largest impact on reducing colonisation rates.
evidence: Comparative conclusion from intervention simulations.

claim: Patient-to-patient transmission (much of which is likely to be mediated by contacts with healthcare workers) is the main driver of resistant K. pneumoniae acquisition.
source: Taken together with the lack of persistent environmental contamination (Smit et al., 2018) and the lack of improvement in model fit when long-term environmental contamination was considered, these findings add support to the view that patient-to-patient transmission (much of which is likely to be mediated by contacts with healthcare workers) is the main driver of resistant K. pneumoniae acquisition, and that colonised patients represent the primary reservoir.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of evidence including modeling and genomic data.

claim: Colonised patients represent the primary reservoir for resistant K. pneumoniae.
source: Taken together with the lack of persistent environmental contamination (Smit et al., 2018) and the lack of improvement in model fit when long-term environmental contamination was considered, these findings add support to the view that patient-to-patient transmission (much of which is likely to be mediated by contacts with healthcare workers) is the main driver of resistant K. pneumoniae acquisition, and that colonised patients represent the primary reservoir.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of evidence including modeling and genomic data.

claim: The rates of transmission within the ward were insufficient to maintain endemic transmission (i.e. the ward-level reproduction number, RA<1).
source: Under the assumption that patient-to-patient transmission was driving the epidemic, we calculated that the rates of transmission within the ward were insufficient to maintain endemic transmission (i.e. the ward-level reproduction number, RA<1) (Cooper et al., 2004).
evidence: Inference from transmission modeling and reproduction number calculation.

claim: Repeated importation into the unit is needed to maintain endemicity of resistant Klebsiella.
source: The findings from both studies indicate that repeated importation into the unit is needed to maintain endemicity of resistant Klebsiella.
evidence: Inference from reproduction number being less than 1.

claim: Control measures should be coordinated regionally and targeted to the wider hospital patient referral network.
source: The public health implications are therefore that control measures should be coordinated regionally and targeted to the wider hospital patient referral network (Donker et al., 2012; Ciccolini et al., 2013).
evidence: Public health recommendation based on study findings and supported by citations.

claim: Antibiotics lead to reduced microbiome diversity and subsequently increase the risk of colonisation with drug-resistant bacteria.
source: These effects are consistent with hypotheses about antibiotic therapy leading to reduced microbiome diversity and subsequently increasing the risk of colonisation with drug-resistant bacteria, which face less competition from fitter, sensitive strains (Lipsitch et al., 2000).
evidence: Mechanistic hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: The greatest dysbiosis following antibiotic therapy in healthy adults is four days after treatment starts.
source: Microbiome analysis has shown that the greatest dysbiosis following antibiotic therapy in healthy adults is four days after treatment starts (Palleja et al., 2018), lending confidence to our model comparison selecting a 96 hour exposure period over a 48 hour period (Table 2).
evidence: Statement supported by microbiome study citation.

claim: The small estimate for α relative to β in transmission model two suggests that background selection plays a relatively small role in acquisition compared with person-to-person transmission.
source: While we cannot differentiate the effects of antibiotics on i) increasing the susceptibility of an infant to acquisition from another infant, versus ii) endogenous selection for resistant bacteria within that infant (Lipsitch and Samore, 2002) in the risk factor models, the small estimate for α relative to β in transmission model two suggests that background selection plays a relatively small role in acqusition compared with person-to-person transmission (Table 3).
evidence: Inference from parameter estimates in transmission model.

claim: Breast milk feeding is associated with development of a healthy gut microbiome in the early stages of life.
source: This accords with our understanding of the development of a healthy gut microbiome in the early stages of life, which can be adversely affected by the replacement of breast milk by formula (Bäckhed et al., 2015), and the protective effect of a diverse microbiome that competes against potentially pathogenic bacteria (Langdon et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to microbiome studies.

claim: A diverse microbiome has a protective effect that competes against potentially pathogenic bacteria.
source: This accords with our understanding of the development of a healthy gut microbiome in the early stages of life, which can be adversely affected by the replacement of breast milk by formula (Bäckhed et al., 2015), and the protective effect of a diverse microbiome that competes against potentially pathogenic bacteria (Langdon et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to microbiome study.

claim: An imbalance between workload and staffing levels may lead to reduced attention to basic infection control measures such as hand hygiene.
source: First, an imbalance between workload and staffing levels may lead to reduced attention to basic infection control measures such as hand hygiene, as has been reported in several studies (Pittet et al., 2006).
evidence: Mechanistic explanation supported by citation.

claim: As nurse:patient ratios decrease, a lower proportion of patient contacts will be cohorted as each nurse will need to contact more patients in a shift, substantially increasing the potential for cross-transmission.
source: Second, as nurse:patient ratios decrease a lower proportion of patient contacts will be cohorted as each nurse will need to contact more patients in a shift, substantially increasing the potential for cross-transmission (Archibald et al., 1997; Austin et al., 1999; Hugonnet et al., 2004).
evidence: Mechanistic explanation supported by citations.

claim: Neonates within a single hospital ward constitute a highly heterogeneous population in terms of acquisition risk.
source: From our model estimates, we observed considerable variation in the risk of acquisition per patient day, with the median posterior probability varying nearly eight-fold from 0.047 to 0.35, showing that even neonates within a single hospital ward constitute a highly heterogeneous population.
evidence: Inference from modeling results showing variation in risk.

claim: The heterogeneity in acquisition risk challenges the assumptions of compartmental models for nosocomial transmission that treat patients as broadly homogeneous.
source: This challenges the assumptions of compartmental models for nosocomial transmission that treat patients as broadly homogeneous in their risk of acquiring drug-resistant bacteria (Grundmann and Hellriegel, 2006; van Kleef et al., 2013; Domenech de Cellès et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference about modeling implications supported by citations.

claim: The Klebsiella carriage population reflects repeated introductions of diverse isolates which were then either spread around the ward over a number of weeks or were not transmitted and became locally extinct.
source: This indicates that Klebsiella in carriage did not reflect a single population, but rather repeated introductions of diverse isolates which were then either spread around the ward over a number of weeks or were not transmitted and became locally extinct.
evidence: Inference from genomic diversity analysis.

claim: Within-host diversity has the potential to hinder the reconstruction of transmission networks.
source: Within-host diversity has the potential to hinder the reconstruction of transmission networks (Worby et al., 2014; Didelot et al., 2016), and our results here highlight the importance of capturing within-host diversity in sequencing studies.
evidence: Statement supported by citations and study findings.

claim: The study highlights the importance of capturing within-host diversity in sequencing studies.
source: Within-host diversity has the potential to hinder the reconstruction of transmission networks (Worby et al., 2014; Didelot et al., 2016), and our results here highlight the importance of capturing within-host diversity in sequencing studies.
evidence: Inference from study findings about within-host diversity.

claim: The study provides strong evidence for person-to-person within ward transmission of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. mediated by healthcare workers.
source: In summary, this study provides strong evidence for person-to-person within ward transmission of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. mediated by healthcare workers, estimates key epidemiological parameters, quantifies the role of different antibiotics in driving the epidemic, and highlights interventions with the potential to contribute to control efforts.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple lines of evidence in the study.

claim: The study quantifies the role of different antibiotics in driving the 3GC-R K. pneumoniae epidemic.
source: In summary, this study provides strong evidence for person-to-person within ward transmission of 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. mediated by healthcare workers, estimates key epidemiological parameters, quantifies the role of different antibiotics in driving the epidemic, and highlights interventions with the potential to contribute to control efforts.
evidence: Summary of study findings.

claim: The study was conducted in a neonatal intensive care unit in a children's hospital in Siem Reap, Cambodia between September 2013 and September 2014.
source: We used data collected prospectively from a neonatal intensive care unit in a children's hospital in Siem Reap, Cambodia between September 2013 (when the neonatal unit newly opened) and September 2014.
evidence: Description of study setting and timeframe.

claim: Rectal swabs were taken within 48 hours of admission and subsequently every two to three days.
source: The study protocol required rectal swabs to be taken within 48 hours of admission and subsequently every two to three days.
evidence: Description of study methodology.

claim: 317 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. isolates were whole-genome sequenced from rectal or environmental swabs over a four month period.
source: We whole-genome sequenced 317 cultured isolates identified morphologically as 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. from i) rectal swabs from all colonised patients within a four month period of the study and ii) twice weekly swabs from seven environmental surfaces around the ward (6 sinks and one computer keyboard) within the same time frame.
evidence: Description of genomic sequencing methodology.

claim: Environmental swabs were taken twice weekly from seven surfaces around the ward (6 sinks and one computer keyboard).
source: We whole-genome sequenced 317 cultured isolates identified morphologically as 3GC-R K. pneumoniae s.l. from i) rectal swabs from all colonised patients within a four month period of the study and ii) twice weekly swabs from seven environmental surfaces around the ward (6 sinks and one computer keyboard) within the same time frame.
evidence: Description of environmental sampling methodology.

claim: Sequencing was performed with the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform, producing 150 base-pair paired-end reads.
source: Sequencing was performed with the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform, producing 150 base-pair paired-end reads.
evidence: Description of sequencing methodology.

claim: The 21 ST101 carriage isolates had a mean read depth ranging from 25x to 125x (median 57x).
source: The 21 ST101 carriage isolates had a mean read depth ranging from 25x to 125x (median 57x), and the 17 ST45 carriage isolates had a mean read depth ranging from 20x to 67x (median 56x).
evidence: Sequencing quality metrics from the study.

claim: The 17 ST45 carriage isolates had a mean read depth ranging from 20x to 67x (median 56x).
source: The 21 ST101 carriage isolates had a mean read depth ranging from 25x to 125x (median 57x), and the 17 ST45 carriage isolates had a mean read depth ranging from 20x to 67x (median 56x).
evidence: Sequencing quality metrics from the study.

claim: All the carriage isolates in both ST45 and ST101 had >90% of the genome covered by >5x coverage.
source: All the carriage isolates in both STs had >90% of the genome covered by >5x coverage.
evidence: Sequencing quality metrics from the study.

claim: Statistical models were fitted using Hamiltonian Markov chain Monte Carlo in Stan within the R environment.
source: We fitted the statistical models using Hamiltonian Markov chain Monte Carlo in Stan (version 2.17.3) within the R environment (v. 3.4.3).
evidence: Description of statistical methodology.

claim: The half life of carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae inoculated onto hospital surfaces is around 12 hours.
source: Studies have shown the half life of carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae inoculated onto hospital surfaces to be around 12 hours (Weber et al., 2015); this corresponds to λ=1.39 in our model.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The agent-based model was implemented in Python and hosted at https://github.com/tc13/ward-infection-ABM.
source: We forward simulated the impact of interventions using an agent-based model implemented in Python (v. 2.7.15) and hosted at https://github.com/tc13/ward-infection-ABM (copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/ward-infection-ABM).
evidence: Description of computational methodology and code availability.
